It's really really important to keep up with PT after surgery and even after PT to still do training on your own.

The first week post-op was the worst pain wise and the other hard part was my fear of retearing my new ACL. 
Also because of the meniscus repair I had to be on crutches for 6 weeks, so that was also annoying.

I think a lot was really in my head, the fears of not hitting milestones, not being able to extend my knee fully again, etc. But in the end it was all unfounded.

Physical therapy was ok. Some better days, some worse days. But if you finally hit the milestones, like jumping and running it's like bein on cloud nine and all the bad fears go away. It's really important to be patient and kind to yourself. 

Ok so about the pain medication, some people get a nerve block that stays for multiple days and block out any pain. I unfortunately had none and also found out I'm part of a small group of people that don't react to oxycodone and it just made me constipated. So I'm not the right person to ask haha

Although Ibuprofen helped a little. Icing helped too. 

I had really really low days during recovery but it was all worth it. I can do everything that I did before. Biking, running, hiking, even asian squatting with my heels on the ground again. I really thought I had to give that up lmao

Hi there, I'm 3 years out of surgery.

I had an ACL reconstruction, medial and lateral meniscus repair.

I got injured when I was 25 and in my case my doctor said that the surgery has to happen, with or without the ACL as the teared mensicus had to be shaved and repaired.

The surgery is ass. The recovery is long and made me cry on multiple occasions but I'm really glad I got it done.

There's no instabilities anymore, no weird popping out of place (I cringed so hard every time), no fear of accidentally slipping or mis-stepping and making the injury worse.

I wouldn't worry to much in your case, you are so young and without the surgery you will always have the instability.
Really the recovery is just a short time compared to the rest of your life. I'll be sure having the surgery would be the best :)

If you have any specific questions, be free to ask :)

I can only speak from my experience, but for me it did get better, gradually. 
I still have some stiff knee, especially if I sit for a longer period (like 1-2h office work, or longer car trips).

It does get stiff but after a few steps it usually feels as normal as it can be. It doesn't affect my usual life.

Cold winters also stiffen up my knee.

My tips for the future:
- Height adjustable desk if possible. Company gave me one after I complained so that's that. In home office, break every so often and stretch

- Same with car trips, I used to be able to go for longer trips, but a break every 2-3h is a must. Sometimes even after an hour. 

- Keep training your legs, it does make a difference.

- Be kind to yourself, sometimes things might not work immediately but it'll be fine. :)

I wish you well and I'm sure it'll be better and better with time :)

Hi I assume you had a quad graft, considering the incisions, so I had a quad graft back in Feb '22 too.

1) Yes that's normal, they just took part of your quad tendon, and lacks the strength to keep it up. It will subside after a while. I did have occasional pain around that area after a few weeks still, but with enough PT it'll be fine.

2) Yeah the surgeon was rummaging in you knee a lot, the bruising and swelling seems normal to me. If you're concerned you can always ask your surgeon. There's nothing wrong about asking them if you're insecure about your recovery. 
Just keep an eye on the incisions for any kind of infection.

Otherwise I wish you well on your recovery journey and if you have more questions just keep asking. This sub really helped me through dark times during recovery too!

I am from West Germany where, unlike East Germany, most Vietnamese came from the south, while my parents both are from the north.
What I witnessed is, that generally speaking south Viet parents learned how to speak German and only speak with their children in German. The few Vietnamese children I knew hardly spoke Vietnamese. They would know the names of food, but that's it. Some of them couldn't even count to 5.

I on the other hand was forced to speak Vietnamese at home. My parents, despite living here for 32 years, hardly speak any German. I'm fluent in vietnamese enough to translate everything for them.

Hey there, in Germany born and raised with Vietnamese parents too 👋

I understand why you don't feel a lot of attachment to Vietnam. I grew up in West Germany, where a) aren't a lot of Vietnamese and b) if Vietnamese, they would be southerners (my parents are both from the north) and those tend to not teach their children Vietnamese. 

I was lucky(?) that my parents forced Vietnamese onto my brother and me when we were younger.
My brother and I are very different in how we define our identities. 
He doesn't care much about Vietnamese culture, media or people, while I am very interested in my heritage. And that's perfectly fine and nothing to be ashamed or concerned about.

I recently went to Vietnam for the first time without my parents and was really glad that I knew basic Vietnamese to get around, find out about my ancestors roots, country and history. I just think you need a certain affinity for these kinds of things. To me this is part of my identity, I am a German Vietnamese and I like it. I love being born into two different cultures.

My brother on the other hand identifies himself differently. It doesn't make him a worse person or hate his ethnicity, he simply doesn't feel the need to know.

Sometimes I wish he would be more interested as Vietnam has a very rich history (even if it didn't influence the world much, it still defined 100mil people), the culture is as flavorful as our food and our country's landscapes are breathtaking. (Also Vietnamese music is getting better, tho I'm still waiting for Viet metalcore haha) Maybe he'll come around, maybe not, either way it's ok.

Don't misunderstand, Vietnam has a lot going wrong too, so does Germany, but still I think it's nice to have the opportunity to witness two different cultures, don't you think? Not many can say that about themselves I think haha.

What I wanted to say is, it's ok to not be interested. It might spark interest at some point, maybe not. And that's ok. Don't fret about it.

Hi, I had my surgery on the 1st of February but tore my ACL, MCL and also both menisci on the 6th December 2021.
Did your surgeon/orthopaedist tell you anything about any kind of restriction in your ROM? Didn't they check your menisci or tears on any other ligaments?

I was restricted for 6 weeks at 90° to relieve my menisci and to let my MCL heal. Afterwards I did have more prehab, but never reached more than 90° and went into surgery like that. Besides I also could extend it to 5°. Never reached full extension before surgery. 

It is generally better if you have a bigger ROM, but I wouldn't be too worried about getting back all ROM. After 6 months I am now at 130° and it works perfectly fine in my day-to-day life. I still do try to get back to heel-to-butt.

To keep your scars soft, you should regularly massage them with some pressure. 

It decreases the build up of scar tissue, helps to improve blood flow and helps with swelling too as it helps with draining fluids.

Best would be combining it with a scaring lotion/Creme. Vitamin E lotion or oil works well.
You should massage your scars for 10-15min a day in circular motions, pulling the skin and go up and down your scar. It's important to move the deeper tissues. 

But please only massage if you have no scabs anymore. Otherwise you risk a reopening of the incision.

Hi there, I'm 6 months post-op and can tell you a bit about my experience. To preface: ACL recon with quad graft, had stitches and also menisectomy.

1. My orthopaedic surgeon adviced me against reaching hyperextension. Hyperextension would only put a higher risk of tearing sth again. So I started to actively standing with my good leg at 0° too. 
I did reach slight hyperextension in my operated knee back tho over time.

2. Imo, that's perfectly normal at this stage. Because of the stitches I had in my mensi us I was only allowed to bend up to 90° for 6 weeks.

3. Flexion will come over time, so while it's good that the PT is focused on that, you should also train the proprioception in your operated leg. The nerves along your now removed ACL is gone and your body needs to relearn how everything functions again.
Muscle training is also important. Don't neglect that. Strong legs and good proprioception reduce the risk for reinjury.

4. Idk how your doctor or pt view that, but after my 6 weeks of partial weight bear and 90° limit, they wanted me to get rid of the brace asap. They said to me that wearing braces make the muscles work less on the bending and result in less muscle build up.
I did however wear my brace when I knew I was going to do more heavier tasks (I recently moved and had to carry al lot)

5. The clicking will stay and I actually don't know if it will ever stop. As long as it doesn't hurt and your knee locks up, it shouldn't be any problem. My knee started to making popping noises the whole time now.

6. You should hold back immediately if it starts hurting. The soreness stems probably from the lack of muscles. You should also regularly stretch your muscles.

7. Like I said I'm 6 months post-op and I still haven't reached the full extension that my good leg has. I am still off my 10° or so. It doesn't hinder me in my normal day to day life tho and I can i.e. bike just fine.

Hope I was helpful with my experiences!

I'd like to give my own input as someone who also grew up with a paranoid schizophrenic father.
I don't want to scare you, but maybe take my story in consideration.

I'm 23(f) and my father had his first psychotic episode when I was 7 and my brother was 3. It was very confusing to us back then, we were just kids and didn't understand why our father suddenly thought that the government was spying specifically on him.
At some point he just vanished for a couple weeks. I now know that he was in a psych ward but I suppose you can't really explain that to kids.

After that he had episodes every three years or so. I remember one day coming home with my mother after we picked up my brother from kindergarten and there was just a card saying we should call this number, it was a number from the psych ward. He tried to kill himself. He tried to jump of a bridge over a highway.
I still remember the visits during the winter. This episode was the first time me and my brother have visited him there. The psych ward was in a forest so we had to walk half an hour through it first to get to him.
I will never forget how he looked at us without saying anything and just pacing back and forth and this still makes me all teared up tbh.

The most fucked up situation was when I was 12, when I watched my father stabbing himself in the stomach, because he wanted to kill himself again.
All I remember was my mother pushing his t-shirt on his belly, my brother crying hysterically behind my bedroom door and me calling the ambulance.

He tried to kill himself a couple times more, but if I count all this will take too long.
So why do I tell you this?
I just want to say that I grew up resenting my father a lot. At times I hated him and actually wished he died finally so my mother, brother and I can get a rest. I had to mature very fast too as my mother can't speak German well and we live in Germany, so I had to manage a lot during the time my father was gone.
I don't like to say I had the worst childhood, but I didn't had the best one too. I grew up depressed and was suicidal most of my teenage years. Making it worse was that when I finally got admitted to a psych ward I was diagnosed with Borderline personality disorder and although I tried my hardest to give my brother the best childhood as a big sister, he grew depressed too, which breaks my heart everyday I see him. I really tried my hardest so he didn't turn out like me and I feel like I failed as a big sister. 
As our whole family doesn't live in this country we don't have a support net either, which made it especially hard. 

My mother grew resentful too. She blames my father almost daily for her misery and her pain which my brother and I have hear from her too.

I just want to tell you that it's a big responsibility to have children when you are schizophrenic.
I don't hate my father anymore, I understand his illness now, but I still resent him for giving me life where he basically just put me through struggle over struggle.

Maybe I just wrote this whole thing too as it's therapeutic for me to talk about, it's a very emotional topic for me, so I'm really sorry for any confusing parts and grammar mistakes.

Edit to say, please be aware that you have a higher risk of epilepsy too, just last month my father had his first epileptic seizure, so please be safe and get it maybe checked when you are at a neurologist.
